U032: Is temporal evidence leakage a valid prior for version contamination, or do the two metrics measure different failure modes with different base rates?

This is a conceptual/metric-comparison question. I can resolve it by analysis of the definitions, with evidence:
- Leakage definition (TempFinRAG): evidence not yet public at the as-of date — an information-boundary violation (too-new evidence). Quote: "a disclosure may support a query only after becoming public" (C033) and "enforces the information boundary defined by U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing availability".
- Version contamination (proposed): a passage not in force at the target date — this includes superseded (too-old) and not-yet-in-force (too-new). The "too-new" side overlaps with leakage; the superseded side is distinct and has no analogue in leakage (under leakage, older evidence is fine since it was public). Also leakage is at the evidence-item level (public availability), while version contamination is at the version-selection level where near-duplicates compete. So they're related but not equivalent: leakage is a subset-ish of one direction of contamination.

So U032 is resolvable as a conceptual/metric taxonomy: they are different failure modes with partial overlap in the "not-yet-in-force" direction. Base rates cannot be transferred; the 10.8% leakage prior should not calibrate the version-contamination threshold. Confidence high-ish (0.75) — this is an analytic definitional claim supported by the abstract-level definitions plus the legal review's bitemporal distinction (valid time vs transaction time), which is the underlying distinction: leakage is about transaction/availability time, contamination about valid time.

That's a strong framing: leakage = transaction-time violation; version contamination = valid-time violation. The legal review discusses valid vs transaction time (C020 quote: "from transaction time, when a norm was recorded in the official system"). So I can cite that.

So U032 → resolved (definitional/conceptual analysis): they are different metrics; leakage is an availability (transaction-time) boundary violation, version contamination is a valid-time/version-selection error; they overlap only where the correct version is one not yet in force. Base rates are not transferable; the Stage-0 threshold must be set independently (or use the oracle-gate headroom rather than an exogenous prior).

Now the step is PLAN_EXPERIMENT and asks for an experiment plan. What plan? A plan to empirically separate the two failure modes: measure both metrics simultaneously on the same retrieval runs and decompose them. That is a concrete, cheap, valuable plan: "Dual-metric decomposition: valid-time version contamination vs availability leakage" — compute both metrics per query, report their correlation, their disagreement cases (superseded-but-old vs not-yet-in-force), and the base rates. This directly reduces U032's remaining empirical part (base rates).

So E005: "Dual-metric decomposition of availability leakage and valid-time version contamination".

Details:
- RQ: On amended legal text, do availability leakage (evidence not yet available at target date) and valid-time version contamination (passage not in force) have the same base rates and the same system ranking, or do they diverge?
- Hypothesis: They diverge: leakage is small and concentrated on not-yet-in-force versions, whereas contamination is larger and dominated by superseded versions; systems ranked by one metric are not ranked the same by the other; the 10.8% financial leakage prior cannot be transferred.
- Method: For each query-passage pair, compute two labels: is the passage in force at the target date (valid time), and was the passage publicly available at the target date (transaction/availability time; for legal corpora use the publication/entry-into-public-record date). Decompose retrieval errors into four cells: (in force & available) correct; (not in force, available) superseded; (in force, not yet available) — impossible/edge; (not in force, not yet available) not-yet-in-force. Report base rates per cell per retriever, plus correlation between the two metrics, and rank agreement.
- Baselines: same retrievers.
- Metrics: leakage rate, contamination rate, superseded share, not-yet-in-force share, correlation/rank agreement, four-way cell counts.
- Datasets: same curated chains; requires availability dates (publication dates) in addition to validity dates.
- Hardware: CPU.
- Failure conditions: metrics identical (rank correlation 1, base rates equal) → transferable; or availability dates unavailable → can't compute leakage.
- Expected outcomes: divergence; contamination ≫ leakage for superseded clauses.

No execution spec.

input.statement: Temporal evidence leakage and version contamination are different failure modes and their base rates are not interchangeable. Leakage is an availability, or transaction-time, violation: it asks whether an item was public at the as-of date, so it is violated only by evidence that is too new and is never violated by old evidence. Version contamination is a valid-time error about which version governs: it is violated both by superseded versions (too old) and by not-yet-in-force versions (too new). The two overlap only in the not-yet-in-force direction; the superseded direction that dominates amended-clause retrieval has no counterpart in the leakage metric, and leakage is defined over evidence availability rather than over competition between near-duplicate versions of the same clause. Therefore the 10.8% leakage figure cannot calibrate a version-contamination threshold, and the Stage-0 stop/go threshold must be justified by the oracle-gate headroom or by an independently measured baseline rather than by that prior.

ablations: Availability definition: official publication date vs entry into force vs first appearance in the snapshot, to test sensitivity of the leakage rate
Chain depth and age gap, since superseded-direction errors should grow with chain depth
With and without near-duplicate version pairs to test whether version competition drives contamination beyond availability effects
Target-date granularity, since day-level as-of dates should sharply separate the two metrics
baselines: Published three-signal hybrid with decay (strongest directly comparable)
Recency-only ranker (isolates the too-old failure direction)
Oracle availability filter and oracle valid-time gate separately, to show the ceiling for each metric independently
confounders_addressed: The two metrics may be near-identical if availability and validity dates coincide for most items - addressed by reporting the date difference distribution and by analysing cases where they diverge
Contamination could be inflated by the corpus containing only current versions - addressed by requiring superseded versions to be present and reporting per-version availability
Reader noise is irrelevant here because both metrics are computed from retrieval outputs only
Query-stratum composition could drive divergence - addressed by computing both metrics per stratum
Availability dates may be missing for many versions - addressed by reporting coverage and restricting the leakage metric to chains with verifiable availability dates rather than imputing
controls: Both metrics computed from the identical frozen per-query rankings
Per-version validity and availability dates verified by hand with provenance recorded
Same candidate pool, k and chunking across retrievers
Per-stratum reporting with confidence intervals and sample sizes
Strict and lenient definitions of both violations reported
Threshold decisions for the broader programme taken from the oracle-gate headroom, not from either extrinsic prior
datasets: The curated clause version chains from Stage 0, augmented with two dates per version: a validity interval (in force from/to) and an availability date (when the text entered the public record)
Required subset: chains where availability and validity dates differ, which are the informative cases for separating the metrics

Optional comparison arm: a static regulatory corpus with documents but no version relations, where version contamination is undefined and only leakage-style measures apply, to show the metrics are not interchangeable
Not used: financial filings and ESG disclosures, whose availability regimes differ from legislative publication
input.expected_outcomes: The two metrics have materially different base rates and different system rankings. Contamination is expected to be substantially larger than leakage and dominated by the superseded direction, while leakage is small and concentrated on not-yet-in-force versions; the recency-only ranker should show near-zero leakage on older queries but high contamination by selecting latest versions; rank agreement between the two metrics is expected to be low. This decomposition also yields the independently measured contamination baseline that the Stage-0 stop/go threshold requires.
failure_conditions: The two metrics produce statistically indistinguishable rates and rank systems identically - the 10.8% prior would then transfer and the dual-metric framing collapses to one metric
Availability dates cannot be recovered for enough versions, so leakage cannot be computed on the legal corpus and the comparison is impossible
Contamination turns out to be a strict subset of leakage on this corpus, meaning no superseded-direction failures occur - the amended-clause premise weakens sharply
Divergence exists but is driven entirely by a handful of chains with anomalous metadata - the result is a metadata artifact rather than a metric distinction
input.hardware: CPU-only: indexing and embedding a few hundred clause versions with BM25 and BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, plus rule-based metric computation. No GPU, no reader LLM, no external API.
input.hypothesis: Availability leakage and valid-time version contamination measure different failure modes with different base rates: on amended legal clauses, contamination is dominated by superseded versions and is substantially larger than leakage, the two metrics rank retrieval configurations differently, and the 10.8% financial leakage rate is not a valid prior for the legal version-contamination rate.
metrics: Availability leakage rate - fraction of retrieved passages not yet public at the target date
Version contamination rate - fraction of retrieved passages not in force at the target date

Decomposition into four cells per retrieved passage: in force and available; not in force but available (superseded); in force but not yet available (edge case); not in force and not yet available (not-yet-in-force)
Rank agreement (Kendall tau) between system orderings induced by the two metrics, with bootstrap intervals
Distribution of the gap between availability date and validity start date per version
Metadata coverage: fraction of versions with verifiable availability and validity dates
Contamination of each retriever minus contamination under the oracle valid-time gate (headroom), for threshold setting
input.proposed_method: Augment each clause version with two date attributes: its validity interval (in force from/to) and its availability date (when the text entered the public record or the corpus snapshot). For every retrieved passage, compute a four-way label combining in-force status at the target date (valid time) with public availability at the target date (transaction time). Run the standard retriever set on the Stage-0 query set, then compute both metrics from the identical frozen rankings, decompose contamination into superseded and not-yet-in-force components, and compare system orderings under each metric. Use the oracle valid-time gate headroom to set the Stage-0 threshold instead of importing the financial leakage prior.
input.reproducibility_notes: No execution spec is attached: no public implementation of a clause-versioned legal retrieval benchmark exists, and the adjacent RMA repository is an interactive notebook over a static, non-versioned corpus requiring third-party PDFs and an API key, with no JSON metrics output. The study is CPU-only and rule-based, so it is cheap to replicate; release the chain metadata (validity intervals, availability dates, provenance for each), the query set with strata, every frozen per-query ranking, the four-way labelling code, and the strict and lenient violation definitions, together with the date-gap distribution used to judge whether the two metrics can diverge on this corpus.
input.research_question: On amended legal text, do availability leakage (retrieved evidence not yet public at the target date) and valid-time version contamination (retrieved passage not in force at the target date) produce the same rates and the same system rankings, or do they decompose into distinct failure modes with different base rates?
input.title: Dual-metric decomposition: availability leakage versus valid-time version contamination on amended clauses
workloads: Queries whose target date precedes the availability of the latest version (leakage-prone)
Queries targeting a superseded version's validity window (contamination-prone, superseded direction)
Queries whose target date lies between availability and entry into force, if such gaps exist (the informative overlap case)
Near-duplicate version pairs, where version competition rather than availability is the failure channel
Deep chains, where repeated supersession should accumulate the superseded-direction error

input.confidence_basis: Definitional analysis grounded in verified statements of how the financial system enforces an information boundary and in the legal distinction between valid time and transaction time. The remaining uncertainty is empirical (actual base rates on a legal corpus), which the recorded plan measures.
input.resolution: Resolved as a definitional matter, with the base-rate question delegated to measurement. Leakage is a transaction-time, availability violation - violated only by evidence too new to have been public - whereas version contamination is a valid-time, version-selection error, violated by superseded versions (too old) as well as not-yet-in-force versions (too new). The superseded direction, which is the distinctive failure in amended-clause retrieval, has no counterpart in the leakage metric, and leakage is defined over availability of an item rather than over competition between near-duplicate versions of the same clause. The 10.8% financial leakage rate is therefore not a valid prior for the legal contamination rate and must not calibrate the Stage-0 threshold; the threshold should come from the oracle-gate headroom or an independently measured legal baseline. Plan E005 measures both metrics jointly to quantify the divergence.

input.description: The dual-metric decomposition requires two dates per clause version: a validity interval and a publication/availability date. Consolidated legal databases expose the former but the latter may exist only at document level, may be recorded differently (official journal publication versus entry into force versus corpus ingestion), or may be missing for older versions, which would make the leakage metric uncomputable and force the comparison to be dropped or approximated.
input.question: Are per-version publication or availability dates (distinct from validity dates) recoverable at clause granularity from public legal corpora?
input.rationale: Without availability dates the leakage side of the decomposition cannot be measured and the comparison between the two metrics collapses to a definitional argument only.
